Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I should have protected others and I failed

vignette: The burning aid station still dictates Sameer’s reality. He had been organizing evacuations when shelling collapsed the makeshift tent, sending him scrambling through choking fire and the deafening shouts of panicked, grieving crowds. When a plume of smoke drifts from a neighborhood barbecue or a colleague’s voice sharpens into anger, that sensory cue immediately pulls his torso back into the soot-stained position of that night, leaving him unable to sequence what happened first. These involuntary flashbacks confirm his crumbling conviction that the world operates on chaos and that he failed to protect the civilians trapped inside. Because he believes he is fundamentally broken and set apart, he instinctively turns away from funerals and graves, covering his face with his hands to block out the world. By deliberately avoiding positive events and retreating to isolated corners, he denies himself any corrective experience, keeping his traumatic recall trapped in a fragmented loop. This self-imposed distance only deepens his isolation and reinforces his belief that he should have done more. The narrowing of his daily routine makes him hyper-aware of any approaching anger or distant smoke. His shattered worldview has rewired his nervous system; the conviction that he failed and that safety is an illusion keeps him awake, scanning the dark long after his wife falls asleep. This relentless night vigilance makes him jump at ordinary household sounds, which in turn exhausts his capacity to focus, leaving the event’s timeline perpetually disjointed. The confusion of his recall deepens his conviction that he should have protected others, and this mounting shame makes him hyper-aware of any approaching anger or smoke. He knows that if he allows himself to feel hopeful, he will be punished, so he actively avoids moments of joy. The narrowing of his daily routine makes him more sensitive to ordinary sounds, which heightens his night vigilance. Now thirty-five, Sameer navigates the fluorescent silence of his tax consulting office, but his daily environment has become a minefield of avoided triggers. When the office coffee machine hisses or a client’s tone rises, he jumps, his concentration shattering as he instinctively covers his face with his hands. He avoids positive department gatherings, fearing that any moment of happiness will be stripped away, and this avoidance keeps his traumatic memories fragmented and his belief that he failed unchallenged. He finally sought help because the isolation has left his marriage emotionally barren, and he is most afraid that his avoidance will permanently erase his capacity for trust. He hopes to finally separate the present from the past, to stop hiding his face, and to believe that the world can be rebuilt.
